Cannabis has needed a prescription to buy since 25 June 2025, and smoking it in public can bring a fine of up to 25,000 THB. Vapes and e-cigarettes are illegal to bring in, own or use, with fines of thousands of baht and no exception for tourists. Alcohol has been on sale from 11:00 to 24:00 since late May 2026 (licensed entertainment venues, hotels and international airport terminals are exempt from the hours), and the legal drinking age is 20.

Last checked: November 2026. Thai drug and alcohol rules have changed several times since 2022 and are still changing: a stricter cannabis control bill was approved by Cabinet on 22 September 2026 and is now before parliament. This page is general information, not legal advice.

Quick rules

  • Don't buy cannabis without a Thai prescription, and never smoke it in public.
  • Don't bring, carry or use a vape, e-cigarette or heat-not-burn device.
  • Don't take cannabis or any drugs out of Thailand, even in transit.
  • Don't buy alcohol before 11:00 or after midnight in shops, or on Buddhist holy days at 7-Eleven.
  • Don't drink and ride or drive; checkpoints are common on Samui's ring road.
  • Don't smoke on designated non-smoking beaches such as Bophut.

Cannabis in 2026

Thailand removed cannabis from its narcotics list in June 2022, and thousands of shops opened. Since then the rules have tightened step by step:

  • Prescription only: since 25 June 2025, cannabis flower is a controlled herb. Buying it requires a prescription from a licensed doctor, dentist, pharmacist or Thai traditional medicine practitioner, and each prescription is limited to a 30-day supply. Recreational sale and advertising are banned.
  • Licensed outlets only: a 2026 ministerial regulation limits sales to licensed hospitals, clinics, pharmacies and registered herbal shops, with record-keeping and inspections. Under the government's plans, shops that are not set up as medical outlets will have to convert or close as their licences expire between 2026 and 2028. More than 7,000 shops had already closed nationwide by early 2026.
  • Public use banned: smoking cannabis in public is treated as a public nuisance, with fines of up to 25,000 THB and/or up to 3 months in prison.
  • Age: under-20s, pregnant and breastfeeding women may not buy or use it.
  • Extracts: extracts with more than 0.2% THC by weight remain Category 5 narcotics.
  • Coming next: on 22 September 2026 the Cabinet approved a draft cannabis control bill that would limit cannabis to medical use, require shops to become medical facilities with a doctor on site when their licences come up for renewal, and set stricter penalties. It now goes to the House of Representatives.
  • Tougher enforcement: in October 2026 the government also proposed amending the Narcotics Act to toughen penalties for cannabis offences, including possession of small quantities. The Public Health Ministry was told to inspect licensed shops and revoke licences for breaches, and Customs to step up checks on cannabis leaving the country.

Our advice is simple: it is illegal to buy without a prescription, and you should never smoke in public, including on the beach, at your villa's pool in view of neighbours or on a boat trip. Never take cannabis, edibles or CBD products out of Thailand: travellers have been arrested at Thai airports and in transit countries.

Vapes and e-cigarettes

Thailand bans the import, sale, possession and use of vapes, e-cigarettes, pods, e-liquids and heat-not-burn devices. The UK government's travel advice is explicit: there are no exceptions for tourists or for personal use. The Tourism Authority of Thailand warns that anyone caught can be arrested and face jail or a fine of several times the value of the items.

  • Penalties: confiscation, fines, and possible detention or a court case. Tourists can be held in Thailand until a case is resolved.
  • Customs: bringing vapes into Thailand is a customs offence, and devices are confiscated at airports.
  • On-the-spot demands: there have been repeated reports of people, sometimes claiming to be police, demanding large cash payments from tourists caught vaping in other resort areas in 2026. If you are stopped, ask for an official receipt and contact the Tourist Police on 1155.
  • Seen for sale on Samui? Vapes are still sold illegally in some shops and markets. That doesn't make them legal to buy or use.

Leave your vape at home. If you smoke, bring or buy ordinary cigarettes (duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes) and use designated smoking areas.

Other drugs

Thailand has some of the world's toughest drug laws. The UK government warns that possessing Class A drugs can lead to the death penalty, and that even small quantities can bring heavy fines or prison. Prison conditions are harsh. Police carry out urine tests at party venues and checkpoints, and a positive test counts as drug use even if you took the drug elsewhere.

  • Methamphetamine (yaba, ice), ecstasy, cocaine, ketamine and magic mushrooms are all illegal. "Mushroom shakes" are still offered at some party venues on the islands; they are illegal, and doses are unknown.
  • Kratom was removed from the narcotics list in 2021 but is regulated; don't take it out of the country.
  • Never carry a package for someone else, and pack your own bags.

Drink spiking and party safety

The UK government warns of drink spiking and drug-assisted sexual assaults in tourist areas, affecting both men and women, and says attacks are most common around Full Moon parties and near bars late at night. Keep your drink in sight, don't accept drinks from strangers, stay with friends, and arrange your transport home in advance rather than accepting lifts. From Samui, a licensed return boat is the safest way to the Full Moon Party: the Full Moon Party speedboat costs 1,400 THB return, or charter the Full Moon private speedboat for your group. Entry to the party (about 200 THB) is paid at the gate. More in our Full Moon Party from Koh Samui guide.

Alcohol: hours, places and age

RuleDetails
Sale hours11:00–24:00 every day, since late May 2026. The old 14:00–17:00 afternoon ban has ended
Exempt from the hoursLicensed entertainment venues (bars and clubs keep their licensed hours), hotels, international airport terminals
Drinking age20. Bars and shops can ask for ID; carry a copy of your passport
No sales atTemples and religious sites, petrol stations and their shops, public parks, schools and on public transport
Holy daysNo sales on 5 Buddhist holidays, except at exempt venues (see below)
Penalty for selling outside the rulesUp to 6 months in prison and/or a fine of up to 10,000 THB (for the seller)
Penalty for drinking outside the hoursSince 8 November 2025, customers who drink in a restaurant or shop during the banned hours (now 00:00–11:00) can be fined up to 10,000 THB

The change to 11:00–24:00 was made permanent by a Royal Gazette notice signed by the Public Health Minister in late May 2026, after a 180-day trial. In practice, 7-Eleven and supermarket tills on Samui now sell beer from 11:00 to midnight. Bars and clubs follow their own licence, not the shop hours, which is why Chaweng's nightlife runs well past midnight. Licensed entertainment venues in designated zones of Koh Samui have been allowed to stay open until 04:00 since 15 December 2023, one of five areas (with Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Chonburi and Phuket) in the original scheme. Police can still close venues that serve under-20s or break their licence, and checks on ID are more frequent in high season. Don't drink in temple grounds, and dress respectfully at temples such as Big Buddha.

Bringing alcohol and tobacco into Thailand

The duty-free allowance for each adult arriving in Thailand is 1 litre of wine or spirits and 200 cigarettes (or 250 g of other tobacco). Customs officers at Bangkok airports do check bags, and travellers carrying more than the allowance have been fined and had goods confiscated. Remember: vapes and heat-not-burn sticks are not covered by any allowance. They are banned outright.

Buddhist holy-day bans 2027

Alcohol sales are banned nationwide from 00:01 to midnight on 5 Buddhist holy days. Since May 2025, these venues are exempt if properly licensed: hotels, licensed entertainment venues, similar venues in tourist areas designated by the Public Health Minister, international airport terminals, and designated special events. Ordinary restaurants, shops, supermarkets and 7-Eleven must stop selling.

Ok Phansa falls on the full moon of the 11th lunar month, which is expected to be around 15 October 2027. [check]

There are no Buddhist holy-day alcohol bans in November or December 2026, so Loy Krathong, Christmas and New Year's Eve are unaffected. Stock up the day before a ban day if you are staying in a villa. See our Koh Samui events calendar for festival dates.

Election-day bans

Alcohol sales are also banned around national and local elections and referendums. The Election Commission announces the exact hours for each vote, and they apply across the area holding the election. The pattern in 2026 has been from 18:00 on the eve of polling day to 18:00 on polling day, for advance voting days as well as the main vote, with penalties of up to 6 months in prison and/or a 10,000 THB fine.

We add any election-day ban to our events calendar and the site-wide alcohol notice as soon as it is announced. If you are hosting a villa party or a wedding on an election weekend, buy drinks in advance and ask your venue what it is allowed to serve.

Drink-driving

The legal blood alcohol limit for most drivers and riders is 50 mg per 100 ml (0.05%). A lower limit of 20 mg per 100 ml applies to drivers under 20, drivers with a provisional licence and anyone driving without a valid licence, under rules updated in September 2024. Police set up checkpoints on Samui's ring road, especially at night and around Chaweng, Lamai and the airport, and breath tests are routine. Penalties include fines, licence suspension and possible prison, and insurance won't pay for a crash if you were over the limit.

Samui's roads are dangerous enough sober: steep hills, sand on bends and sudden rain. Take a taxi or Grab after drinking. See Koh Samui roads and is Koh Samui safe?

Smoking on beaches

Thailand banned smoking on 24 popular beaches in 2018, including Bophut beach on Koh Samui, with fines of up to 100,000 THB or up to 1 year in prison for smoking or dropping cigarette butts outside designated smoking areas. Smoking is also banned indoors in bars and restaurants, in national parks (including Ang Thong National Marine Park, which reopens on 16 December after its annual closure) and on many piers and boats. On other beaches, use an ashtray and take your butts with you: they end up in the sea. Cannabis and vapes are illegal on every beach, whatever the tobacco rules.

Alcohol on boat trips and at sea

Drinking and swimming or snorkelling don't mix: alcohol affects balance, judgement and breathing control, and most drownings at sea involve it. Skippers have the final say on board. If you charter a private boat for a celebration, plan swimming stops before the drinks start, and never ride a jet ski or kayak after drinking.

If you are arrested

  • Stay calm and polite. Don't resist, and don't offer cash.
  • Ask to contact your embassy and ask for an interpreter. Don't sign statements you can't read. Embassies can't get you released or pay fines, but they can check on your welfare and give you a list of local lawyers.
  • Call or ask someone to call the Tourist Police on 1155 for help with language.
  • Tell your family and your travel insurer; many policies exclude incidents involving drugs or alcohol. Keep copies of every document you are given.
